zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset (CC BY 4.0). Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used for lexical cross-checks only; the native BnF scan governs the diplomatic text.

lines.note: Nindō is the human realm among the six Buddhist paths. Bup. is the upright Buddhist-domain label; the Portuguese enumeration continues below.

runs.text: eſtados de que ſe falla no

lines.note: The six paths are described as states taught in Buddhist doctrine, with this one identified as the human being. The embedded Buppô has a circumflex and upright type; OCR Buppò misplaced the accent category.
Completes the definition of the human realm as the person inhabiting this world. This is a short continuation of Nindǒ, not an independent entry.
Ningai is glossed first as the human body and then as this world. The printed mũ- begins mundo across the physical line break.

runs.text: do, em que os homens viuem.

lines.note: Do completes mũ-do; the second sense is the world in which human beings live. The gloss does not reduce both senses to the modern word for a person.
Ninjaku is explained by Macaxe tçuqu and by Portuguese weakness or lack of resolution. The printed Japanese paraphrase is retained without imposing modern lexical segmentation.
Ca completes pouca: little decisiveness in matters. Ningiacuna begins the adjectival example describing a person on the following row.

runs.text: Homem froxo, & que não ſe reſolue

lines.note: Fito completes ninjakuna hito, an irresolute person. The Portuguese specifies someone weak who does not readily make up his mind.
Facilmente completes the negative construction above: the person does not resolve matters easily. Its brevity does not make it furniture or a separate entry.
Ninjū, paraphrased hito no naka, means among people. The headword's caron on u is retained independently of the different long-vowel mark in Nindǒ.
Ningu is a strong man, directly matched by homem de forças. The entry is distinct from the following ningue despite their similar opening letters.
Ninge is paraphrased hito ni bakuru, taking human form. The Portuguese makes a demon the transforming subject; demo- continues into demonio below.

Completes the demon's assumption of a human figure. The final S. is an upright written-language label, not part of the italic definition. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ningen is glossed as humankind or the human race. The collective Portuguese wording is preserved rather than narrowed to one individual.
Ningyō, literally a human figure in the accompanying paraphrase, is a statue or puppet. Its marked final vowel distinguishes it from the unmarked ningyo entry two rows below.
Frate completes the divided Portuguese boni-frate, a puppet or jointed figure. It belongs to the preceding statue/doll entry.

runs.text: Sereas que com ſeu canto dizem que

lines.note: Ningyo is glossed through the European comparison with sirens. The text reports what is said about their singing, rather than asserting a zoological observation.

runs.text: fazem dormir aos que as ouuem.

lines.note: The reported effect of the sirens' song is to put listeners to sleep. This completes the relative clause begun in the preceding row.
Ninzen, paraphrased hito no mae, means before or in the presence of people. Maye retains the printed historical spelling.

Ninji here denotes a human matter or work. The upright S. marks written usage and distinguishes this noun entry from the verb immediately below. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
The verb ninzuru means admitting someone into a group or appointing him to a rank. The abbreviated principal parts are retained, and the Portuguese sentence continues below.

runs.text: dos outros, ou aleuantar em dignidade, &c.

lines.note: Completes admission among others and adds elevation in dignity or rank. The historical aleuantar spelling is not modernized.
Hito wo kurai ni ninzuru illustrates appointing a person to a rank. The object and rank expressions are printed as Fitouo and curaini, without editorial spaces inside them.
Completes the translation: raising someone to a dignity or office. This is the continuation of Aleuantar a, not a second example.
This ninjin means the human body, explained by hito no mi. A small but visible i after j restores Ninjin from OCR Ninjn; the three neighboring homographs have different glosses.
This separate ninjin denotes the human heart or mind, matching hito no kokoro. The worn opening of cocoro is interpreted with the surviving letters and the Portuguese heart gloss.

runs.text: Hũa certa erua medicinal que tem a

lines.note: The third ninjin is a medicinal plant, identified by its root in the continuation. The definition should not be conflated with the body and heart entries above.

runs.text: raiz como de cinouras, ou rabãos.

lines.note: The medicinal plant has a root compared with carrots or radishes. Raiz, not OCR ruiz, is visible; the historical cinouras and rabãos are retained without modernizing their vowels or tilde placement.
Nininzure means two people going together. The printed doubled zz and the Portuguese dous remain part of the diplomatic text.
Ninjō here means human compassion, paraphrased hito no nasake. The a of naſaqe is abraded, but the surviving letter spacing does not justify OCR's internal word break; the long ſ is retained.
This distinct ninjō means wounding. The example begins shimobe-domo wo, referring to servants; the scan supports Ximobedomouo rather than OCR Ximobodomouo, and nin- continues the verb below.
Completes ninjōshi and continues with killing the servants, followed by an expression of incomprehension. Xetgai retains the printed checked t; fun- belongs to funbet on the next row.
Funbet ni oyobanu says that the action is beyond understanding. Fei. is the upright source label; L. 2. and the Portuguese translation are italic apparatus.

runs.text: matar os criados, ou ſeruos não o entendo.

lines.note: Completes the translation: the speaker does not understand wounding and killing the servants. The paired criados and ſeruos explains the Japanese shimobe-domo.
Ninju denotes the number of people, paraphrased hitokazu. Its gloss also allows the collective sense people, continued below.
This short continuation supplies the alternative collective gloss people. It is not a new entry and must remain attached in interpretation to Ninju.

This homographic ninju means human life, explained by hito no inochi. The scan reads Ninju, not OCR Nanju; S. is an upright written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ninmin means the common people, with hito and tami as Japanese explanations. The Portuguese distinguishes the populace from an individual person.

Ninniku here means patient forbearance with some humility. The abraded letter after Pa has the surviving curve of c, supporting Paciencia rather than OCR Pariencia; it is unrelated to the garlic homograph below.
This separate ninniku is garlic. The simple Portuguese Alhos establishes the botanical sense without merging it with patient endurance above.
Ninnin, paraphrased hitobito, first has a distributive meaning: each of the people. The alternative gloss continues on the next physical row.
Completes each person and then adds the collective sense men or people. The visible ß-shaped sort in peßoa is retained rather than replaced with modern ss.
Ni no miya denotes the sovereign's second son. The Portuguese uses Rey; the note does not replace the printed royal terminology with a modern institutional title.

runs.text: Braço do cotouelo atè o collo da mão.

lines.note: Ni no ude is described here as the portion from elbow to wrist. That source definition is retained even though a modern reader may associate ninoude with a different part of the arm.

runs.text: O que tem figura de homem não o

lines.note: Ninpinin begins a new entry for something with human form that is not human. Its line begins at the entry margin, so the erroneous continuation indent is removed while the ID is preserved.
Completes the Buddhist nonhuman-being sense before introducing a figurative use. Imagina corrects OCR tmagina; Buppô is upright throughout, with a worn second p but a clear circumflex.

runs.text: per met. Peßoa que ſe não conta nem admi-

lines.note: The figurative sense is a person not counted or admitted among others; admi- continues as admite at the top of column 2. The damaged ß-shaped sort in Peßoa has visible right-hand strokes absent from OCR Peſoa.

runs.text: te entre os outros por pobreza, miſeria, &c.

lines.note: Te completes admi-te from the bottom of column 1: exclusion from other people because of poverty or misery. This is running text, not a repeated catchword.
Ninriki, paraphrased hito no chikara, means human strength. The partly worn chicara remains supported by its surviving letters and the Portuguese plural forças.
Ninsaku is human workmanship or invention. The headword contains long ſ, unlike the short s of the next entry.
Ninsō means a human figure or statue. The visible short s corrects OCR Nineǒ, and Estatua replaces the malformed Estaiua; the human qualification continues below.
Humana completes figura humana. The one-word row belongs to Ninsǒ and is retained as its own physical line.
Ninsoku, alternatively ninbu, is a person carrying goods. Latin l introduces the alternative, while fa- begins Portuguese fato on the following row.
Completes fato, goods or baggage, and compares the carrier with a porter. This clarifies that the entry concerns hired carrying work rather than human strength in general.
Nintai is explained as a person's substance or body. The printed Suſtancia is retained without adding the b of modern substância.

runs.text: no. ¶ Item, Peßoa nobre, ou afidalgada.

lines.note: No completes humano; a second sense is a noble or genteel person. The ß-shaped sort is visible in Peßoa, and the regional qualification follows below.

The X. label marks the regional usage just given, and the text says that in cami the form is Iintai. The scan has one X, not OCR Xx; lowercase cami remains italic as printed, while Iintai is upright and represents jintai rather than a sequence beginning with two vocalic i's.
Ninnō is glossed as king of men, with another sense beginning first king. The visible e restores Rey from OCR Ry; Pri- continues below.
Meiro completes Primeiro, giving the dictionary's second gloss as the first king of Japan. The Portuguese designation is reported without adding an identification absent from this entry.
Ninushi means the owner of the goods or baggage. The rounded capital D and following o support Dono, correcting OCR Bano.
Ninset, paraphrased hito no set, denotes human discourse or teaching. The final checked t is retained rather than expanded to a modern tsu syllable.

runs.text: opinião, & doutrina que decende, ou vem ſò-

lines.note: The definition continues with opinion and doctrine originating from human beings alone. Opinião corrects OCR opimião; the historical decende and divided ſò- remain as printed.
Mente completes ſò-mente, restricting the source of the doctrine to human beings. It is the close of the Ninxet definition, not a new example.
Nippon is Japan, accompanied by the Japanese paraphrase hi no moto. The visible Fino moto spacing and the Portuguese spelling Iapão are retained.
Nippongi is equated with Nifongui and referred to an earlier entry. The editorial i and the Latin instruction remain distinct from the Japanese names.

runs.text: Dous tempos do anno. Como primaue-

lines.note: Niki denotes two periods of the year. The definition begins its paired examples with primaue-, continued as primavera below.
Completes primavera and pairs spring with summer, or autumn with winter. The scan reads eſtio, not OCR's transposed eſito; the printed capitalization of Outono is retained.

runs.text: Crauo, ou eſpinha que nace no roſto.

lines.note: Nikibi is a facial spot or pimple. The historical nasce-less spelling nace and the provisional roſto s/t classification are retained from the print and aligned baseline.
The regional note gives Nicumi as the Ximo form corresponding to nikibi. Ximo is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and remains italic in this impression; Nicumi is the upright cited alternative.

runs.text: Hũa erua como cebolas que ſe come em

lines.note: Nira is an edible onion-like herb. Como is a single printed word, not OCR co mo; the dish in which it is eaten follows on the next row.
Xiru, soup, is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese description of how nira is eaten. Its italic type is retained rather than automatically changed merely because the word is Japanese.
The niramu verb is glossed as looking with fixed eyes. Its historical past-form abbreviation ǒda is retained rather than modernized to nda; the manner of looking continues below.
The eyes are also described as wide open. The example names Benqei looking at Togaxi and divides chōdo between chǒ- here and do below.

runs.text: do nirǒde, nanitaru yaxin chǒbonno mo

lines.note: Completes chōdo nirōde, looking directly or intently, and continues Benqei's challenge about a leader of conspirators. The final mo continues into mono on the next row without a supplied hyphen.
The Japanese challenge ends with the form mexicomeraruruzo and the upright citation label Tog. The translation begins Olhã-, with a visible abbreviation tilde and terminal hyphen, not OCR Olhi-.

runs.text: do Benquei com os olhos reſgalados aquelle homẽ

lines.note: Do completes Olhãdo: Benquei looked wide-eyed at that man. The scan joins aquelle, unlike OCR a quelle; the Portuguese rendering of the Japanese name remains as printed.

runs.text: lhe diße que cabeça, ou capitão de trèdos pren-

lines.note: Continues the challenge about what chief or captain of traitors is being held. The visible ß-shaped sort gives diße, and a small grave is retained in trèdos; pren- continues the verb below.
Deis completes prendeis, and the visible question mark closes the challenge. OCR deisẽ mistook that punctuation for a letter and diacritic.
Niramitsumeru intensifies the fixed stare. The printed principal parts introduce a sustained action, explained across the next row.
The eyes remain fixed and wide open for some time. This duration distinguishes the entry from the preceding general niramu definition.
Nire, alternatively nire no ki, is identified simply as a tree of that name. The source does not provide a botanical description here, so none is inserted into the transcription.
Nisō is explained as two aspects, interior and exterior. The visible t restores Futatçuno from OCR Futarçuno; ex- continues the Portuguese exterior below.
After completing exterior, the example says to perceive the two aspects. Vomote- begins the explanatory Japanese phrase continued on the next row.

The phrase begins with looking at the exterior; the next row glosses knowing the interior. The abraded miyoru is retained after a second enlarged comparison: the rounded vowel and r-shaped type do not securely establish e and n. Miyenu ('unseen') would fit the gloss, but is not supplied without those strokes; miyuru/miyeru are likewise not imposed.

runs.text: Pollo exterior adiuinhar, & ſaber o interior.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains inferring and knowing the interior from the exterior. This supplies the intended relation between the two aspects without authorizing an emendation of the preceding Japanese wording.
Nisoku is glossed as birds; the example combines quadrupeds and bipeds as food. Xo- begins shokusuru at the line break.
Completes shokusuru and translates the example as eating the flesh of birds and animals. Both categories belong to the same example rather than separate definitions.

runs.text: Ir cada dia à Tera, ou di-

lines.note: The intended word is nissan, daily attendance, equated with himairi. No usable i is visible in the abraded gap after N, so N ſsan is retained rather than supplied from the NINJAL lexical aid; Ir cada is visibly two words. Tera occurs within the Portuguese explanation.
Ante completes diante: daily attendance may be at a temple or before one's lord. This continuation completes the two destinations in the previous line.
Nite is first described as an ablative preposition, using the printed Propoſição rather than a modernized grammatical term. Par- begins the second account as a particle.

runs.text: ticula que com outras ſignifica ſendo. Vt,

lines.note: The particle, combined with other words, means being. Yo- starts yoki in the example on the following row.
Completes yoki hito nite, being a good person. The tilde in Sẽdo is preserved rather than expanded in the canonical transcription.
Nitomeku concerns the sticking or adhesion of something. The compressed principal parts and the Portuguese algũa abbreviation remain printed forms, with cou- continuing below.
Completes the description of something soft and sticky. The isolated Nito- beneath this line is the catchword, not a further part of the definition.
